whyItExists.problem: Abrupt visual changes (colour switches, element appearances) feel jarring and cheap. Motion conveys state, guides attention, and provides feedback.
whyItExists.solution: CSS transitions animate between two states smoothly. CSS animations run independently with @keyframes, enabling looping and complex multi-step sequences — all without JavaScript.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Hover effects, focus states, loading indicators, entrance animations, micro-interactions.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Always respect prefers-reduced-motion. Avoid animations that serve no purpose — motion should communicate something. Gratuitous animation decreases usability.

explainModes.beginner: transition makes a CSS change happen smoothly over time instead of instantly. animation plays a sequence automatically — like a flipbook.
explainModes.simple: transition: property duration easing — animates a CSS property change on trigger (:hover, :focus). @keyframes defines a sequence of CSS states. animation: name duration easing — plays that sequence.
explainModes.standard: Transitions need a trigger (state change). animations run automatically or on class addition. Both use easing functions (ease, linear, cubic-bezier). transform and opacity animate on the GPU — prefer them over animating width, margin, or color for 60fps performance.
explainModes.technical: CSS transitions trigger when a property changes value (by pseudo-class, class toggle, or JavaScript). The transition calculates the interpolation between from and to values. Animations use @keyframes with percentage waypoints. will-change: transform hints the browser to promote the element to a GPU layer before animation starts.
explainModes.deepDive: The Web Animations API (WAAPI) exposes CSS animation internals to JavaScript, allowing play, pause, reverse, and speed control. CSS scroll-driven animations (Scroll Timeline, View Timeline — 2023+) animate based on scroll position with zero JavaScript. Both are hardware-accelerated when animating transform and opacity.

content.text: Always check prefers-reduced-motion: wrap all non-essential animations in @media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) { ... }. Some users experience motion sickness from animations.

questions.question: Which CSS property allows an element to transition smoothly to a new state?
questions.explanation: transition animates the change between two CSS states (like normal and :hover). animation uses @keyframes to run sequences automatically.

questions.question: Which CSS properties should you animate for the best performance?
questions.explanation: transform and opacity are composited on the GPU and do not trigger layout or paint recalculation. Animating them produces smooth 60fps animations. Animating margin, padding, width, or top triggers expensive layout recalculations.

faq.q: What is the difference between transition and animation?
faq.a: transition animates between two states triggered by a change (hover, focus, class toggle). animation runs a @keyframes sequence independently — it can loop, have multiple steps, and start automatically without a trigger.

both applies the animation's first keyframe before it starts (forwards fills) and keeps the last keyframe after it ends (backwards fills). Without it, elements snap back to their original state after the animation completes.

faq.q: What is transform: translateY(-3px) and why is it used for hover effects?
faq.a: translateY(-3px) moves the element 3px upward. It is used on hover to create a 'lift' effect that feels tactile. It is GPU-accelerated (unlike margin-top), so it runs at 60fps with no layout cost.

examples: GitHub uses CSS transitions on its button hover states throughout the interface
Stripe's homepage uses complex @keyframes animations for its gradient background
Every modern loading spinner is a CSS animation: spin @keyframes on a border-top-colored circle
